# The Role of Transition-Metal Elements in Quasicrystals and Related Complex Phases

This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the role that transition-metal elements play in quasicrystals and their related complex crystalline phases. Quasicrystals, with their unique long-range order but lack of periodic translational symmetry, present a fascinating class of materials whose physical properties are intricately linked to their atomic and electronic structure. Understanding how specific constituent elements—particularly transition metals—influence these properties is essential for both fundamental scientific understanding and potential technological applications.

## Electronic Structure Considerations

A central focus of this study is the examination of how transition-metal elements affect the electronic structure of these complex materials. Transition metals, characterized by their partially filled d-orbitals, are known to introduce distinctive features into the electronic density of states, including the formation of pseudogaps and resonance states near the Fermi level. This research explores the mechanisms by which these elements contribute to such electronic characteristics, investigating the hybridization effects between transition-metal d-states and the s-p states of other constituent elements. The resulting electronic structure modifications have significant implications for the stability and physical behavior of quasicrystalline phases.

## Transport Property Implications

Building upon the electronic structure analysis, this research further investigates the consequences of transition-metal incorporation on the transport properties of quasicrystals and related complex phases. The unusual electronic structures characteristic of these materials—particularly the presence of pseudogaps at the Fermi level—are known to give rise to anomalous transport behaviors, including unusually high electrical resistivities and unconventional temperature dependencies. This study examines how variations in transition-metal content and type correlate with observed changes in these transport phenomena, providing insight into the underlying physical mechanisms that govern electrical conduction in these structurally complex systems.

## Collaborative Research Contributions

It should be noted that substantial portions of this research were carried out in collaboration with Prof. T. Fujiwara. This partnership proved instrumental in advancing several key aspects of the investigation, combining complementary expertise and methodological approaches to address the complex questions surrounding transition-metal effects in quasicrystalline systems. Furthermore, certain components of this work were originally initiated as a direct outcome of this collaborative relationship with Prof. Fujiwara, underscoring the value of such scientific partnerships in advancing the understanding of these intricate materials systems. The collaborative nature of this research has enriched both the theoretical framework and the interpretive depth of the findings presented herein.

# The Role of Transition-Metal Elements in the Electronic Structure and Transport Properties of Quasicrystals and Related Complex Phases

## Introduction

Quasicrystals represent a fascinating class of materials that exhibit long-range order without translational periodicity, challenging conventional understanding of crystalline structures. Since their discovery, these materials have attracted considerable attention due to their unusual physical properties, including unconventional electronic transport behavior, unique mechanical characteristics, and distinctive electronic structures that differ markedly from those of conventional periodic crystals. Among the various families of quasicrystals studied, those containing transition-metal elements—such as Al-Mn, Al-Cu-Fe, Al-Pd-Mn, and related systems—have proven particularly important for understanding the interplay between local atomic environments and global aperiodic order.

This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the role that transition-metal elements play in determining the electronic structure and transport properties of quasicrystals and their closely related complex crystalline phases, often referred to as approximants. This work builds upon a long-standing collaborative research program initiated with Prof. T. Fujiwara, whose pioneering contributions to the theoretical understanding of quasicrystalline electronic structure have significantly shaped the direction of this field. Through this collaboration, we have sought to develop a more complete picture of how transition-metal d-electron states hybridize with the surrounding sp-electron framework to produce the characteristic electronic and transport signatures observed in these materials.

## Background and Motivation

The electronic structure of quasicrystals is known to exhibit several distinctive features, including a pseudogap at the Fermi level, sharp spiky structures in the density of states arising from quasiperiodic order, and unusually low electrical conductivity despite the metallic nature of their constituent elements. These properties have been attributed to various mechanisms, including Hume-Rothery-like stabilization mechanisms, strong electron-phonon coupling, and the critical role of transition-metal d-states near the Fermi energy.

Transition-metal elements, with their partially filled d-orbitals, contribute significantly to the density of states near the Fermi level in many quasicrystalline systems. The hybridization between these localized d-states and the more extended sp-states of the surrounding aluminum or other main-group matrix elements creates complex electronic structures that are highly sensitive to local atomic arrangements. Understanding this hybridization process, and how it depends on the specific quasiperiodic tiling and local coordination environments, has been a central goal of theoretical and experimental research in this field for several decades.

## Methodology

Our investigation employs a combination of first-principles electronic structure calculations and transport property analysis to elucidate the role of transition-metal elements in quasicrystals and approximant phases. We utilize density functional theory (DFT) based methods to compute the electronic density of states, band structure characteristics, and orbital-resolved contributions from transition-metal d-electrons in various quasicrystalline and approximant structures.

The theoretical framework developed in collaboration with Prof. Fujiwara incorporates realistic atomic structural models for quasicrystals, including large periodic approximants that capture the essential local atomic environments present in genuine quasicrystalline phases. These approximant structures, which possess conventional periodicity but share similar local atomic clusters with quasicrystals, serve as computationally tractable models for understanding the electronic structure of the true aperiodic systems.

Transport properties, including electrical resistivity, Hall coefficient, and thermoelectric power, are calculated using the Kubo-Greenwood formalism and related transport theories, incorporating the calculated electronic structure as input. Special attention is paid to the role of transition-metal d-states in modifying the scattering mechanisms and the energy dependence of the electronic density of states near the Fermi level, both of which critically influence transport behavior in these systems.

## Key Findings

Our results demonstrate that transition-metal elements play a crucial and multifaceted role in shaping both the electronic structure and transport properties of quasicrystals and related complex phases. Specifically, we find that:

1. **Pseudogap Formation**: The hybridization between transition-metal d-states and the sp-states of surrounding atoms is a primary mechanism responsible for the formation of the pseudogap at the Fermi level, a hallmark feature of quasicrystalline electronic structure. The depth and width of this pseudogap are sensitively dependent on the specific transition-metal species and their local coordination environment.

2. **Density of States Structure**: Transition-metal d-orbitals contribute significantly to the fine spiky structure observed in the density of states of quasicrystals, arising from the quasiperiodic arrangement of atoms and the resulting multiple scattering effects. This spiky structure, in turn, has direct consequences for the transport properties, as the Fermi level position within these fine features can dramatically affect the electrical conductivity.

3. **Transport Anomalies**: The unusual transport properties observed in transition-metal-containing quasicrystals, including the increase of electrical resistivity with decreasing temperature (a hallmark of these systems) and the unusually large and sometimes negative Hall coefficients, can be understood in terms of the electronic structure features associated with transition-metal d-states near the Fermi level.

4. **Comparison with Approximant Phases**: By comparing the electronic structures of quasicrystals with their periodic approximant counterparts, we demonstrate that many of the essential electronic features responsible for the observed transport anomalies are already present in the approximant phases, suggesting that local atomic environment, rather than long-range quasiperiodic order alone, plays a dominant role in determining these properties.

5. **Chemical Trends**: Systematic variation of the transition-metal species (e.g., Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Pd) reveals clear chemical trends in the electronic structure and transport properties, providing valuable guidance for the design and interpretation of experiments on new quasicrystalline and approximant systems.

## Discussion

These findings offer significant insight into the fundamental physics governing quasicrystalline and complex phase systems. The central role played by transition-metal d-electrons in determining both the electronic structure near the Fermi level and the resulting transport properties underscores the importance of considering not just the geometric aspects of quasiperiodic order, but also the detailed chemistry and electronic character of the constituent elements.

This work extends and refines the theoretical framework established through our collaboration with Prof. Fujiwara, providing a more nuanced understanding of how transition-metal contributions manifest in real materials. The results have important implications for the broader effort to understand the stability, electronic structure, and physical properties of quasicrystals, and may inform future efforts to design new quasicrystalline materials with tailored electronic and transport properties.

## Conclusion

The investigation presented in this paper substantially advances our understanding of the role of transition-metal elements in quasicrystals and related complex phases. Building on the collaborative foundation established with Prof. T. Fujiwara, we have shown that transition-metal d-electron contributions are central to explaining the characteristic electronic structure features and transport anomalies observed in these fascinating materials. These findings not only deepen our fundamental understanding of quasicrystalline physics but also provide a valuable framework for future theoretical and experimental investigations into this rich and continually evolving field of condensed matter physics.
